headline: An algorithm identifier is compared as the bytes a root program fixed, not as the algorithm it names.
summary: The Mozilla Root Store Policy states its algorithm requirements as exact DER, because two identifiers naming the same algorithm can differ in whether the parameters are an explicit NULL or absent, and only one of those is admitted. The policy ships as `mozilla-root`. Unlike every other profile here it is named and never detected: a root program's requirements apply because the certificate chains to a root in that store, which the certificate does not state and a single-certificate lint cannot know.

Added: `pki.lint.certificate(der, { profile: "mozilla-root" })` runs the Mozilla Root Store Policy v3.1 profile. Naming it is the only way to reach these rows, and passing no profile leaves every one of them inert.

The section 5.1 algorithm encodings, compared as DER: a subjectPublicKeyInfo AlgorithmIdentifier must be one of the four the policy writes out, for RSA and for NIST P-256, P-384 and P-521, and a signature AlgorithmIdentifier one of the ten, covering RSASSA-PKCS1-v1_5, RSASSA-PSS at its matching mask and salt lengths, and ECDSA. Only one of a certificate's two algorithm fields is read, because the parser already refuses a certificate whose outer `signatureAlgorithm` differs from `tbsCertificate.signature`.

An RSA modulus must be at least 2048 bits and a whole number of octets, and a public exponent of 1 is reported as the unusable key the policy names. An EdDSA key is admitted only in a certificate carrying `id-kp-emailProtection`, and is exempt from the encoding rows, since the policy gives no EdDSA encoding to hold it to. An EdDSA signature is exempt for the same reason and on the issuer's behalf: a permitted EdDSA intermediate signs with that key, and reporting the certificates it signs would fail them for a key they do not carry.

The section 5.1.3 SHA-1 prohibitions, each gated to the date it carries: from 1 July 2022 over an end entity certificate carrying `id-kp-emailProtection`, and from 1 July 2023 over a certificate carrying `id-kp-OCSPSigning` or over an intermediate certificate. That clause names intermediates rather than certificate authorities, so a root's own self-signature is not one of the four things it lists. The clause also allows SHA-1 over an end entity only where a list of conditions all hold, so a certificate carrying no extKeyUsage, or one naming `id-kp-serverAuth` or `anyExtendedKeyUsage`, is reported as outside that allowance. Its remaining conditions name the issuing certificate and the Baseline Requirements scope, which are not in these bytes.

The section 5.2 practices a certificate's own bytes answer for: an extKeyUsage extension on every end entity certificate with no `anyExtendedKeyUsage` in it, and a serial number greater than zero. The rest of that sentence asks for at least 64 bits of CSPRNG output, which constrains the draw rather than the integer, and a DER INTEGER drops the leading zero octets a draw produces: eight random octets beginning with zero encode to seven of magnitude, which a conforming certificate does about once in 256. So a short magnitude is reported as a warning and the positive-serial half as an error, each at the strength its own clause supports.

The section 5.3 rules for intermediate certificates created after 1 January 2019, gated to that date: an extKeyUsage extension is required, `anyExtendedKeyUsage` is not permitted, and `id-kp-serverAuth` and `id-kp-emailProtection` may not appear together. Being an intermediate is a role in a hierarchy that a certificate does not state, so these three read the one thing the bytes give and pass over a certificate issued in its own name. That is every root, which the clause does not govern, and it is also a rollover intermediate reissued in its own name, which the clause does govern, so the three under-report rather than reporting a root for carrying no extended key usage.
Changed: `pki.lint.rules()` enumerates the new rows, which stay inert under the default rule set because each one asks whether the caller named the profile.
